n: Saul fully approved of Stephen’s killing. That day a severe persecution breaks out against the Jerusalem church, and believers scatter through Judea and Samaria — though the apostles stay. Persecution begins to fulfill Acts 1:8.

f.w: Saul was consenting unto his death
throughout the regions of Judæa and Samaria

n: Devout men bury Stephen and mourn deeply for him — openly grieving a man executed by the council took courage.

f.g: lamentation = loud mourning, wailing.

n: Saul tries to destroy the church, going house to house and dragging men and women off to prison.

f.g: Greek for ravaging, like a wild animal mauling prey.
haling = hauling, dragging.

n: But the scattered believers preach the word wherever they go. Scattering the seed only spreads it further.

f.w: went every where preaching the word

n: Philip — one of the Seven, not the apostle — goes to a city of Samaria and proclaims Christ there. Jews and Samaritans had been bitter rivals for centuries.

f.g: Samaritans accepted only the five books of Moses and worshipped at Mount Gerizim.

n: The crowds listen attentively to Philip as they hear his message and see his miracles.

f.g: united, all together.

n: Unclean spirits leave many people with loud shrieks, and many who are paralyzed or lame are healed.

f.g: palsy = paralysis.

n: The city is filled with joy. The gospel brings joy wherever it is received.
A man named Simon had long practiced magic there, amazing the Samaritans and claiming to be someone great.

f.g: Practiced magic arts. Later tradition calls him “Simon Magus.”
bewitched = amazed, astonished.

n: Everyone, from least to greatest, followed him, calling him “the Great Power of God.”

f.g: A title suggesting people saw him as divine or a divine emanation.

n: They followed him because his magic had impressed them for a long time.

f.g: for a long time.

n: But when they believe Philip’s message about God’s kingdom and Jesus Christ, men and women alike are baptized.

f.w: they were baptized, both men and women

n: Even Simon believes and is baptized. He follows Philip closely, astonished by the genuine miracles he sees.

f.g: His later behavior shows his conversion was incomplete.

n: When the apostles in Jerusalem hear that Samaria has accepted God’s word, they send Peter and John — the same John who once wanted to call fire down on a Samaritan village.

f.w: they sent unto them Peter and John

n: When they arrive, they pray for the new converts to receive the Holy Ghost.

f.w: that they might receive the Holy Ghost

n: Luke explains that the Holy Ghost hadn’t yet come on any of them; they had only been baptized in the Lord Jesus’s name. Baptism of water and of the Spirit are distinct ordinances.

f.w: only they were baptized in the name of the Lord Jesus
f.g: Latter-day Saints have understood that Philip held authority to baptize but not to confer the Holy Ghost, which required the apostles’ higher authority.

n: Peter and John lay hands on them, and they receive the Holy Ghost — the ordinance Latter-day Saints call confirmation.

f.w: laid they their hands on them
f.r: Acts 19:5-6; Articles of Faith 1:4; D&C 33:15; Moroni 2:2

n: Seeing the Spirit given through the laying on of hands, Simon offers the apostles money.

f.g: The word “simony” — buying or selling church offices — comes from Simon’s name.

n: He asks them to sell him the power to give the Holy Ghost by laying on hands. He sees priesthood as a marketable skill.
Peter rebukes him sharply: “May your money perish with you,” for thinking God’s gift could be bought.

f.w: the gift of God may be purchased with money

n: Simon has no share in this ministry, because his heart isn’t right before God.

f.g: No share or portion at all.

f.w: thy heart is not right in the sight of God

n: Peter urges him to repent and pray, in hope that the intent of his heart might be forgiven. The door to repentance stays open.

f.w: Repent therefore of this thy wickedness

n: Peter perceives that Simon is full of bitter poison and bound by sin.

f.g: gall = a bitter, poisonous substance.

n: Simon asks them to pray for him that these warnings won’t befall him. Luke leaves his final fate unknown.

f.w: Pray ye to the Lord for me

n: Peter and John testify and preach, then head back to Jerusalem, preaching in many Samaritan villages along the way. The old wall between Jews and Samaritans is breaking down.

f.w: preached the gospel in many villages of the Samaritans

n: An angel tells Philip to go south to the desert road that runs from Jerusalem down to Gaza. Leaving a thriving work for an empty road requires faith.

f.g: An ancient Philistine city near the Mediterranean coast, on the route to Egypt.
Either the road or old Gaza was deserted, a lonely route.

n: Philip goes, and meets an Ethiopian official — a eunuch in charge of the treasury of the Candace, queen of the Ethiopians — who had traveled to Jerusalem to worship.

f.g: Ancient Ethiopia (Kush) lay south of Egypt, in what is now Sudan.
A royal title (Kandake) of the queen mother of Kush, not a personal name.
Eunuchs were barred from full temple worship under the law, but Isaiah foresaw their welcome among God’s people.

n: Riding home in his chariot, he is reading aloud from the prophet Isaiah.

f.g: Esaias = Isaiah. Ancient people usually read aloud; a scroll of Isaiah would have been costly.

n: The Spirit tells Philip to go up and walk alongside the chariot.
Philip runs to it, hears the man reading Isaiah, and asks, “Do you understand what you’re reading?”
“How can I, unless someone guides me?” the official replies humbly, and invites Philip to sit with him.

f.w: except some man should guide me

n: He was reading Isaiah 53: like a sheep led to slaughter and a lamb silent before its shearer, he did not open his mouth.

f.w: He was led as a sheep to the slaughter

f.g: dumb = silent.

n: In his humiliation justice was denied him; who can speak of his descendants, for his life was taken from the earth?

f.g: Abinadi explains that Christ’s “seed” are those who follow the prophets and look to him for redemption.

n: The official asks: is the prophet speaking about himself or someone else? It’s exactly the right question.

f.w: of whom speaketh the prophet this?

n: Starting from that very passage, Philip tells him the good news about Jesus.

f.w: began at the same scripture, and preached unto him Jesus

n: As they travel they come to water, and the official asks, “Look, here is water. What prevents me from being baptized?”

f.w: what doth hinder me to be baptized?

n: Philip says he may if he believes with all his heart, and he confesses that Jesus Christ is the Son of God. This verse is missing from many early manuscripts but reflects early baptismal practice.

f.w: If thou believest with all thine heart

n: He stops the chariot, both go down into the water, and Philip baptizes him — a description that fits baptism by immersion.

f.w: they went down both into the water

n: When they come up out of the water, the Spirit of the Lord suddenly takes Philip away. The official never sees him again but goes on his way rejoicing. Christian tradition credits him with helping bring the gospel to Africa.

f.w: the Spirit of the Lord caught away Philip
he went on his way rejoicing

n: Philip turns up at Azotus and preaches in every town along the coast until he reaches Caesarea, where he later settles with his family.

f.g: The old Philistine city of Ashdod.
Caesarea Maritima, the Roman capital of Judea on the Mediterranean coast.
